questions.q: Why does a traditional rowstore clustered index work poorly for a fact table's typical workload?
options: Fact tables are scanned and aggregated across millions of rows, not looked up by a single key value, which a row-by-row B-tree doesn't optimize for
SQL Server does not allow clustered indexes on fact tables
Fact tables never have a primary key to index
Rowstore indexes only work on dimension tables
questions.explain: A fact table's typical query is an aggregate scan (SUM/GROUP BY across many rows), which a traditional row-by-row index doesn't help and can actively slow down.

questions.q: What is the default, recommended index choice for a fact table in a SQL Server data warehouse?
options: A clustered columnstore index
No index at all
A unique nonclustered index on every column
A full-text index
questions.explain: A clustered columnstore index stores the fact table column-by-column with heavy compression and batch-mode execution, which matches the aggregate-scan workload fact tables see.

questions.q: What actually happens when you run CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX on a table?
options: It converts the entire table's physical storage to the columnstore format — it's not an index added alongside an existing heap or B-tree
It creates a second, unrelated copy of the table
It deletes all existing rows in the table
It only affects how SSMS displays the table's icon
questions.explain: A clustered columnstore index IS the table's storage — there is no separate rowstore heap or B-tree underneath it once created.

questions.q: When would you choose a nonclustered columnstore index instead of converting a fact table to a clustered columnstore index?
options: When the table still needs fast single-row rowstore lookups alongside analytical queries, so it stays rowstore with a columnstore index covering just the analytical columns
Never — nonclustered columnstore indexes are not a real SQL Server feature
Only on dimension tables, never on fact tables
Whenever the table has fewer than 100 rows
questions.explain: A nonclustered columnstore index lets a table keep its normal rowstore clustered index for lookups while still getting columnstore's batch-mode benefit on the columns it covers.

questions.q: Why are dimension tables typically indexed with ordinary rowstore indexes instead of columnstore indexes?
options: They're usually much smaller than fact tables and are queried by lookups and joins, not large aggregate scans
SQL Server does not support columnstore indexes on dimension tables under any circumstances
Dimension tables never have a primary key
Columnstore indexes are only legal on tables with fewer than 10 columns
questions.explain: Dimension tables (thousands to low millions of rows) are queried by lookups and joins, which a normal clustered rowstore index on the surrogate key handles well.
